\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more information.

Prior work found trace utility to be task-dependent \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks where output noise confounds the analysis.
Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, and controlled component ablation directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning.
This approach aligns with recent *CL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.

We present a systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we evaluate four models across three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

The central result: complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone (${\sim}$73--76\%) while exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models and seeds (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
A simple regex baseline (B5) that exploits the \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} format marker matches this ceiling at 99.33\%; even a trivial pattern suffices, so the interesting question is not why exceptions help but \emph{why complete traces hurt}.
Marker removal collapses B5 to 28.49\% while SFT retains 97.65\% ($-$2.01pp); bidirectional cross-dataset transfer (99.4--100\%) shows that SFT acquires language-level diagnostic patterns beyond format matching (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

A controlled gradient masking ablation attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution; content quality (diagnostic signal density at inference) accounts for the majority, though forward-pass attention is an unquantified residual (\S\ref{sec:density}).
Training dynamics support this: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps, while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates between 82--89\% without stable convergence (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp performance jump at ${\sim}$512 tokens; this threshold coincides with the globals module dump (${\sim}$384 tokens), beyond which structured \texttt{[Line~X]} variable values appear (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

A cross-model budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a sharp performance jump localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens.
At tail-384, all models remain near baseline (73.6--80.7\%, only +1.0--4.8pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512 (+13.2--22.0pp), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling (${\sim}$94--98\%).
This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, crossing the globals module dump threshold (${\sim}$384 tokens) and exposing structured execution markers (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).
CodeLlama tail conditions use label-only loss (\S\ref{sec:density}); cross-model tail comparisons should account for this training difference.
Beyond 512 tokens, accuracy converges further: multi-seed validation across all 12 model$\times$seed combinations confirms all tail-512 accuracies fall within a 4.63pp band [93.61\%, 98.24\%] (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}); at tail-1024, three models reach 96.5--98.2\%, compressing the 6.3pp cross-model spread observed at tail-256.
\texttt{tail\_2048} captures 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy across all completed configurations.
The residual 2--5pp gap confirms that semantic extraction (identifying exception type and message) still outperforms positional extraction (retaining a fixed window containing non-diagnostic lines).

\paragraph{Calibration.}
\label{sec:calibration}
Calibration mirrors the tier hierarchy: \texttt{exception\_only} achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for \texttt{no\_trace}, a 63$\times$ gap (Figure~\ref{fig:calibration}).
This calibration advantage generalizes across architectures and scales: all four models (1.5B--13B) achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.005 under \texttt{exception\_only} (Table~\ref{tab:calibration_model_level} in Appendix), indicating well-calibrated predictions rather than overfit confidence.

\paragraph{Error analysis.}
\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors have zero overlap with all other conditions' error sets (Jaccard = 0.000; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_overlap}); per-type breakdown confirms all standard exception types achieve 100\% accuracy, with only \texttt{GeneratorExit} (a benign \texttt{BaseException} subclass) causing failures (Appendix~\ref{sec:exception_type}).

\paragraph{Length control.}
Padding \texttt{exception\_only} to 2{,}048 tokens, even in a semantically loaded position (after the verdict region), yields identical accuracy (99.83\%), indicating the 18--23pp gap arises from spurious patterns in verbose trace content, not sequence length.

\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}

DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, confirming complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).

A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.

Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).
